summary: Slice 023B (WP-SCP-023 per-repo scorecard emitter, HEAD b5f6e54) presents 0 CRIT, 1 MAJ, 2 MIN, and 2 nit safety/bypass findings. All 11 primary verification points were checked exhaustively. The emit-generation responsibility is correctly within the SCP reusable workflow (not adopter-controlled code). The schema enforces additionalProperties: false at every nesting level — no waiver content fields (reason, approved_by, waiver_id) can appear. The Python heredoc reads only expires_at and rule_id from each waiver entry; no waiver content is serialised. yaml.safe_load is used throughout. CODEOWNERS covers all five newly-touched file paths. Schema-version drift mitigation is documented in the schema description, D-041, and the plan-doc risk register. Pre-023C opt-in is safe (artifact is inert until the aggregator lands). The three plan-doc §4 threat boundaries are unchanged. MAJ-SAFE-001: the workflow-level permissions comment at lines 59-70 makes the materially false claim that 'Adopters who do not opt in see no behaviour change' with respect to the new permissions — the id-token: write and attestations: write ARE granted to ALL runs of the reusable workflow, including non-scorecard-emit runs. The id-token: write permission allows any step in any policy-check run to request a GitHub OIDC token asserting the SCP reusable workflow identity; adopters who configure cloud IAM to trust this workflow identity (an increasingly common GitHub Actions OIDC pattern) expose their cloud resources to any compromised step in all policy-check runs, not just opt-in ones. The 'marginal blast-radius reduction' dismissal of job-level scoping understates this OIDC trust-chain risk. MIN-SAFE-001: the broad except (ImportError, Exception): rc = {} in the rule-config parse block silently produces false-negative scorecard data (rc_disabled_rules = []) without emitting any ::warning:: annotation, making the aggregator see a clean rule-config when the actual file may be malformed. MIN-SAFE-002: SCP_WAIVERS_PATH and SCP_RULE_CONFIG_PATH accept adopter-supplied string inputs without constraining them to the workspace directory; Path().read_text() is called on these unconstrained paths, opening an arbitrary filesystem read surface. Content is never included in the emit (only counts), so practical impact is limited, but reading /proc/self/environ or large device files is possible. nit-SAFE-001: the SHA pin for actions/attest-build-provenance@a2bbfa25375fe432b6a289bc6b6cd05ecd0c4c32 (v4.1.0) cannot be independently verified in a read-only review; the operator must confirm via gh api repos/actions/attest-build-provenance/git/ref/tags/v4.1.0. nit-SAFE-002: ImportError is a subclass of Exception so the explicit ImportError clause in except (ImportError, Exception) is redundant.

findings.claim: The workflow-level permissions comment at lines 59-70 of policy-check.yml makes the materially false claim that 'Adopters who do not opt in see no behaviour change' in relation to the new attestations: write and id-token: write permissions. These permissions are set at the workflow (not job) level and are granted to ALL runs of the reusable workflow regardless of whether the scorecard-emit input is true or false. The comment's dismissal of job-level scoping as producing only 'marginal blast-radius reduction' understates the real threat: id-token: write allows any step in ANY policy-check run to request a GitHub OIDC token asserting the SCP reusable workflow identity (jrnb2024/standards-control-plane-/.github/workflows/policy-check.yml). Adopters who configure cloud IAM roles to trust this workflow identity — a standard pattern for GitHub Actions OIDC cloud authentication — expose those cloud resources to any compromised step in all their policy-check runs, not only scorecard-emit opt-in runs.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 56-72: permissions block is at the workflow (top) level, not job level. Lines 59-70 comment: 'Adopters who do not opt in see no behaviour change — the action is never invoked.' This statement is true for the actions/attest-build-provenance ACTION (gated at line 1469 on inputs.scorecard-emit), but is FALSE for the id-token: write and attestations: write PERMISSIONS, which are granted regardless of the input. The 'Attest scorecard emit' step at line 1468 has 'if: inputs.scorecard-emit && steps.build-scorecard-emit.outcome == success' — the step is gated, but the permission is not. The comment at lines 67-70 rejects job-level scoping: 'Job-scoping the permission was considered but rejected: the existing policy-check job is the natural home for the emit step, and splitting into a separate gated job would duplicate the runtime-binary install + summary build dependencies for marginal blast-radius reduction.' GitHub Actions OIDC cloud authentication pattern: any adopter who has bound an AWS/GCP/Azure IAM role to this workflow identity (via aud claim matching jrnb2024/standards-control-plane-/.github/workflows/policy-check.yml) would have that IAM role accessible from all policy-check runs, not just opt-in ones.
findings.impact: Non-opt-in adopters (scorecard-emit: false, the default) run a workflow job with id-token: write active. If any step in the SCP reusable workflow is ever compromised — via a malicious vendor binary slipping past SHA256 verification, a zero-day in OPA/Conftest/Regal, or a future careless PR introducing an unsafe action — the compromised step can call getIDToken() and receive a JWT asserting the SCP workflow identity. Adopters who have cloud IAM roles trusting this workflow then have those cloud resources exposed. The blast radius extends across ALL adopter repos on every PR run, not just the subset that opted into scorecard-emit. This is not a theoretical risk: OIDC-based cloud access for GitHub Actions is documented by GitHub, AWS, GCP, and Azure as a recommended pattern for eliminating static credentials. The comment misleads operators into believing the new permissions are inert for non-opt-in runs.
findings.mitigation: Two acceptable mitigations (propose both; choose one): (A) Preferred — move the attestation step to a separate job with job-level permissions (attestations: write, id-token: write), gated on needs.policy-check.result == 'success' AND the scorecard-emit input. The main policy-check job retains only contents: read and statuses: write. The workflow comment should be updated to reflect the actual scoping. File TF-023B-001 to track this split at 023C. (B) If splitting is genuinely too costly — amend the comment to accurately state: 'id-token: write and attestations: write are granted to ALL runs of this reusable workflow, including non-scorecard-emit runs. Adopters who configure cloud IAM to trust this workflow identity should be aware that these permissions are active in every policy-check run. All actions in this workflow are SHA-pinned and binary-verified; the supply-chain controls are the primary defence against misuse of these permissions.' Remove the 'no behaviour change' claim and strengthen the threat-surface argument. File TF-023B-001 for 023C to evaluate job-level scoping with a two-job structure mirroring D-037's release-gate-violation-issue job split.

findings.claim: The broad except (ImportError, Exception): rc = {} at policy-check.yml line 1389 in the 'Build scorecard emit' Python heredoc silently produces false-negative scorecard data when the rule-config YAML parse fails for any reason. When triggered, the scorecard reports rc_disabled_rules = [] (no disabled rules) and rc_expiring_30d = 0, making the aggregator see a clean rule-config state even when the actual .scp/rule-config.yaml is malformed or unreadable. No ::warning:: annotation is emitted.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 1385-1410: 'if rc_path.is_file(): try: import yaml; rc = yaml.safe_load(rc_path.read_text()) except (ImportError, Exception): rc = {}'. The except block catches yaml.YAMLError, IOError, PermissionError, and any other exception. On exception, rc = {} causes rules = rc.get('rules', {}) to return {}, rc_disabled_rules to remain [], and rc_expiring_30d to remain 0. The emit at lines 1412-1430 then includes 'rule_config_aggregate': {'disabled_rules': [], 'expiring_within_30d': 0}, misrepresenting the actual rule-config state. The 'Validate rule-config against schema' step at lines 682-716 would catch most malformed YAML (exits 1 on exception), causing the validate-summary step to see a failed job and the scorecard-emit step to skip (gated on validate-summary.outcome == 'success'). However, there are edge cases where the rule-config passes schema validation but fails to parse in the emit step (e.g., file deleted between steps, symlink race, encoding issue on a non-UTF-8 file). In those cases the broad except is the only handler and it silently degrades the data.
findings.impact: The aggregator at 023C receives a scorecard claiming zero disabled rules, when the adopter's actual rule-config may have several disabled rules. This is a false-negative in estate observability: the aggregator under-reports suppressed rules. The impact is informational (scorecards are observational per plan-doc invariant 1), not a policy gate bypass. However, the purpose of scorecards is accurate estate state; silent data degradation undermines that purpose. An operator reviewing the aggregated index would have no indication that any adopter's rule-config data was incomplete.
findings.mitigation: Replace the silent fallback with a degraded-but-announced fallback: in the except block, emit a ::warning:: annotation before setting rc = {}, e.g.: print('::warning file=.scp/rule-config.yaml,title=SCP-SCORECARD-W001::rule-config parse failed in scorecard-emit step; rule_config_aggregate will be empty. Check for YAML syntax errors or encoding issues.') then rc = {}. This preserves the defensive non-fatal posture (the emit still succeeds) while surfacing the data-quality issue to the PR author and the aggregator operator. File as TF-023B-002 if fix-round timing is tight.

findings.claim: The waivers-path and rule-config-path workflow_call inputs are not validated against the workspace directory boundary. The Python heredoc in the 'Build scorecard emit' step calls Path(os.environ.get('SCP_WAIVERS_PATH', ...)).read_text() and Path(os.environ.get('SCP_RULE_CONFIG_PATH', ...)).read_text() on unconstrained adopter-supplied paths. An adopter can supply absolute paths (e.g., /proc/self/environ, /etc/group) or path-traversal sequences (e.g., ../../../../etc/passwd) to cause the workflow to read arbitrary files on the GitHub-hosted runner.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 1346-1347: 'waivers_path = Path(os.environ.get("SCP_WAIVERS_PATH", "output/findings/waivers.json"))'; lines 1382-1383: 'rc_path = Path(os.environ.get("SCP_RULE_CONFIG_PATH", ".scp/rule-config.yaml"))'. Neither path is validated against the workspace root (e.g., Path.cwd() or GITHUB_WORKSPACE). workflow_call input waivers-path (line 26-30) and rule-config-path (line 31-35) accept arbitrary strings with no path constraint. The same paths are used in earlier steps (Validate rule-config against schema, Enforce break-glass pairing gates) with identical absence of workspace-boundary validation, making this a pre-existing pattern extended to the scorecard-emit step. Path().read_text() on /proc/self/environ would succeed on Linux runners and return environment variables including any GitHub secrets or GITHUB_TOKEN values that were set in the job env.
findings.impact: An adopter can read arbitrary files on the GitHub-hosted runner. However: (1) file CONTENT is never included in the scorecard emit — only counts and rule_id keys are extracted; (2) JSON parse failure on non-JSON files causes wlist = [] with no content leakage; (3) YAML parse failure causes rc = {} with no content leakage; (4) valid rule_id extraction is constrained to the regex SCP-R-[0-9]+ pattern; (5) the adopter already controls the default-path files in their own repo. The practical impact is: (a) potential large-file / device-file reads causing memory pressure on the runner (mitigated by except Exception fallback), and (b) the possibility of artificially inflating waivers_aggregate.active_count by pointing waivers-path at a crafted JSON file elsewhere on the runner or repo. This last case is already possible by modifying the default waivers.json in the adopter's own repo, so the marginal attack surface is low.
findings.mitigation: Add a workspace-boundary check before the Path().read_text() calls. Use the GITHUB_WORKSPACE environment variable as the allowed root: import os; workspace = Path(os.environ.get('GITHUB_WORKSPACE', os.getcwd())).resolve(); then before each read: resolved = path.resolve(); if not str(resolved).startswith(str(workspace)): emit_warning and skip. Alternatively, validate at the workflow input level by adding a fixture-path-style Python validation step (mirroring the existing SCP_FIXTURE_PATH validation at lines 477-490) that rejects inputs containing path-separator sequences outside the workspace. File as TF-023B-003 if deferred.

findings.claim: The SHA pin actions/attest-build-provenance@a2bbfa25375fe432b6a289bc6b6cd05ecd0c4c32 (commented as v4.1.0) cannot be independently verified in a read-only review without external network access. The reviewer cannot confirm that the 40-character commit SHA a2bbfa25375fe432b6a289bc6b6cd05ecd0c4c32 corresponds to the v4.1.0 tag of the actions/attest-build-provenance repository.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml line 1470: 'uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@a2bbfa25375fe432b6a289bc6b6cd05ecd0c4c32 # v4.1.0'. The SHA is full 40-character form (correct pinning format). The human-readable tag comment v4.1.0 is present. Verification requires: gh api repos/actions/attest-build-provenance/git/ref/tags/v4.1.0 and confirming the returned SHA matches. No existing lockfile or manifest in the SCP repo records the expected SHA for this action (unlike OPA/Conftest/Regal which are in scripts/scp-policy-check.lock).
findings.impact: If the SHA does not correspond to v4.1.0 — whether due to a typo, a mis-annotation, or a deliberate substitution — the workflow is running a different version of the attestation action than documented. The attestation action has id-token: write access and attestations: write access; a wrong-version action could behave unexpectedly. Nit severity because the SHA pin IS present (the security control), and the worst case of a misannotated comment is that the comment is wrong, not that an unverified action runs.
findings.mitigation: Operator verification step: run 'gh api repos/actions/attest-build-provenance/git/ref/tags/v4.1.0 --jq .object.sha' and confirm the output is a2bbfa25375fe432b6a289bc6b6cd05ecd0c4c32. If v4.1.0 is a lightweight tag, use '/git/ref/tags/v4.1.0'; if annotated, dereference via '/git/tags/<sha>'. Consider adding actions/attest-build-provenance to a Renovate dependency group or to a future extension of scripts/scp-policy-check.lock so the SHA-tag correspondence is machine-verifiable at PR review time.

findings.claim: The except clause at policy-check.yml line 1389 reads except (ImportError, Exception): rc = {}. ImportError is a subclass of Exception in Python, so the explicit ImportError is redundant — it is already caught by the bare Exception clause. The redundancy creates the false impression that ImportError is being handled distinctly from other exceptions.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml line 1389: 'except (ImportError, Exception): rc = {}'. Python class hierarchy: ImportError -> ModuleNotFoundError (subclass), ImportError -> Exception (superclass chain: ImportError -> Exception -> BaseException). Any except Exception clause already catches ImportError. The intent of listing ImportError separately was likely to handle the case where 'import yaml' at line 1388 raises ImportError (yaml not installed), but since pyyaml is unconditionally installed by the 'Ensure caller-data dependencies' step earlier in the same job (lines 652-680 with hash-pinned install and version assertion), ImportError is effectively unreachable here.
findings.impact: None — the behaviour is identical. Nit severity for code clarity only.
findings.mitigation: Change to: except Exception: rc = {}. Optionally add a comment: # yaml is unconditionally installed by the 'Ensure caller-data dependencies' step; ImportError is unreachable but Exception covers it regardless. This makes the intent explicit without the misleading redundant subclass listing.

self_reported_concerns: MAJ-SAFE-001 severity calibration: the actual exploit path requires (a) a compromised step in the SCP reusable workflow AND (b) an adopter's cloud IAM configured to trust this workflow identity. Both conditions together represent a meaningful but non-trivial attack chain. The finding is classified MAJ because the COMMENT is materially false (it says 'no behaviour change' when the permission IS granted), not solely because of the exploit chain. The comment inaccuracy is a governance violation — operators are misinformed about security posture.

MIN-SAFE-001 and MIN-SAFE-002 both have 'pre-existing pattern' context: the waivers-path/rule-config-path inputs and the broad except pattern exist in earlier workflow steps (Enforce break-glass pairing gates, Emit expired-rule-config warning). Flagging them here is correct because 023B extends their reach to the new scorecard-emit context, but fixing them in isolation in 023B without addressing the same patterns in the earlier steps would be inconsistent. The mitigations should be applied consistently across the workflow. A TF for the earlier steps is appropriate.

Check (6) on the actions/attest-build-provenance SHA (nit-SAFE-001): the action signs the artifact upload metadata via GitHub's Artifact Attestation API using the OIDC token. The aggregator at 023C verifies via gh attestation verify --signer-workflow, which checks the job_workflow_ref OIDC claim against the SCP reusable workflow path per D-042 and plan-doc §5. This is the correct mechanism. The review cannot confirm the SHA-tag correspondence without network access; this is a known limitation of the read-only review posture.

The plan-doc §5 sample JSON at docs/plans/WP-SCP-023-cross-repo-scorecards.md includes a 'signature' field in the sample emit shape, but the implemented schemas/scorecard-emit.schema.json has additionalProperties: false and does NOT include a 'signature' property. This is intentional (per the schema description: 'no in-payload signature field — platform-level attestation is the trust anchor') and correct per the DISPATCH-NOTE OUT section ('OIDC attestation generation in the emitter step' deferred to 023C in-payload form). However, the plan-doc sample is stale and could confuse future adopters. This is a correctness finding outside the safety lens; noting it here for the correctness R1 reviewer.

The bypass_emitted field from policy-check-summary.json is intentionally NOT included in the scorecard emit (not in the schema). When break-glass bypass is active, the scorecard will show verdict: deny (because the deny finding exists in the summary) with the bypassed rule's denies > 0. This is correct estate-observability behaviour: the aggregator accurately sees the repo is non-compliant, even though the PR was allowed through. No safety finding here — noting for transparency.
